prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities and monetary policy: staggered price and wage setting, policy rules for evaluating monetary policy, and a microfounded framework for its analysis

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged: B001 with Taylor, Woodford and Calvo as a single achievement. The chair asked what separates these three from Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets. My criterion is origin of the idea, identifiable in specific papers, with a separate test of whether the idea changed how a field reasons. Calvo supplied the tractable time-dependent pricing device. Taylor supplied staggered contracts and the policy-rule approach to evaluating monetary policy. Woodford supplied the integrated welfare-based theory of policy. The other five names built the canonical empirical model, identified estimation, and central-bank adoption. That work is important, but it extends and quantifies the originating ideas. The criterion is applied the same way across fields, and it is the standard I would apply to any candidate. It would change the laureate set if the Committee instead decided the discovery was identified estimation of DSGE models. That would be a different citation. I would not choose it, because it would make the prize depend on the empirical record of the descendants, which is the contested part. On the post-2021 inflation, state-dependent pricing and heterogeneity, I treat the evidence as mixed and not as validation. State dependence limits the claim that Calvo pricing describes firm behaviour. It does not remove the benchmark role of the originating ideas, so I would keep the citation on those ideas. The ideas date from 1979 to 2003, so there is no timing risk, and no recent prize covers this core. My assessment rests on general knowledge and the supplied ballot text, not on independent verification.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem is real. Any three-name cut excludes people with strong claims, and the proposed laureates cover three different types of contribution (pricing device, contracts and rule, synthesis). That is a weaker unity than a single paper or a single programme. The empirical record is mixed: Phillips-curve fit, evidence on state dependence in price adjustment, and the 2021 to 2023 inflation. Earlier macro prizes (Lucas, Kydland and Prescott, Sargent and Sims) narrow the unclaimed space. Priority questions involving Fischer, Phelps and Rotemberg, who is tied to the Woodford synthesis but is not on the ballot, are unresolved. The Taylor rule can be read as policy prescription more than science. If the Committee cannot settle attribution, B006 has a cleaner trio and B021 a cleaner pair, and I would support either with the laureate sets below.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first and sees Calvo, Taylor and Woodford as origin points. He treats Galí, Gertler and Christiano-Eichenbaum as mostly codifying, estimating and extending the structure. He says he would not move to Galí or Gertler unless the Committee wanted to reward estimation and quantification.
responses.response: I agree with the origin-point logic and I use it as my separating criterion. I do not go as far as his reading of the inflation episode, where he sees extension rather than damage. I read the evidence as mixed, and I would not let the award depend on it. The citation should therefore name the ideas (pricing, contracts and rules, microfounded policy framework) and make no claim about forecasting performance. I also note that his field proximity to heterogeneous-agent macro is disclosed. That literature builds on this framework and does not replace it, and I do not treat that proximity as bearing on the merits.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B001 first and accepts that the credit is broader than any trio. He raises whether the Taylor rule is science or prescription, and priority questions involving Fischer and Phelps. He also notes that Gertler overlaps with the 2022 prize and with B002.
responses.response: I take the Taylor rule point seriously, and it affects the wording of my citation. I credit Taylor for staggered contracts and for the policy-rule framework as a way to evaluate and compare policy, which is an analytical contribution, and not for the particular coefficients. The citation now says 'policy rules for evaluating monetary policy' to reflect that. I agree that Fischer and Phelps raise priority questions that the three-name cap cannot settle. I would state openly that the citation recognises specific contributions and does not settle all priority. I also agree that crediting Gertler would blur the macro allocation. The Calvo, Taylor and Woodford set avoids the Gertler overlap with B002.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, ranks B002 first with Kiyotaki and Moore as the cleanest two-person attribution. He concedes that its identification is mostly from later work by others and that B001 is the natural alternative if policy influence outweighs attribution clarity.
responses.response: I accept that Kiyotaki and Moore have the cleaner attribution in macro, and that attribution clarity is a legitimate criterion. On the same common criteria, I still put B001 ahead for two reasons. Its ideas have been used directly in institutional practice for decades. And, as he notes, B002 rests on calibrated models and later work for its empirical content, as well as sitting closer to the 2022 recognition of banks and financial crises. I would not oppose a B002 award on scientific grounds. I note that the chair's preference is disclosed and that I do not treat it as evidence of merit.

responses.point: Teorell prefers B006 and argues that its attribution is cleaner than B001 because Persson, Tabellini and Besley form the recognisable core of one programme. He also argues that the 2024 institutions prize answered a different, causal question.
responses.response: I agree that the B006 attribution is cleaner, and I said so in round 1. I accept his distinction from the 2024 prize, and I do not count that prize as decisive. My remaining difference is about evidence. The B006 framework is conceptually strong, but the constitutional-effects results rest on cross-country variation, as he concedes. B001's originating contributions rest on specific papers, and their influence on practice is easier to document. That is a weighing of different criteria, not a claim that B006 is weak. If B001 stalls on attribution, I would support B006 with Persson, Tabellini and Besley.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B021 first. He says Melitz 2003 and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work form a core with a clean two-person attribution. He also says the framework has been tested on firm-level data for over twenty years and builds on, rather than is replaced by, quantitative trade models.
responses.response: This part of his argument changed my alternatives list. In round 1 I listed B015. In the opening I ranked B021 fourth, so my view of it has not changed. What has changed is my judgement of attribution risk. B015's Bresnahan versus Levinsohn question is unresolved and only four members ranked it. B021 has a two-name core that Boppart and Fredriksson both say the Committee can word around the selection model. As someone who tests theory on hand-collected micro data, I value that the framework meets firm-level evidence. I share the concern about Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum sitting outside the entry, and I would keep the citation narrow.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee accepts excluding Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets from a three-person prize. I would not support adding Galí in place of Calvo unless the Committee decides the discovery is the canonical empirical New Keynesian model.
How much the post-2008 and post-2021 record, and the evidence on state-dependent pricing, should count against the framework as opposed to its originating ideas.
Whether the Taylor rule is judged scientific or only practical, and how the Committee resolves priority questions involving Fischer, Phelps and Rotemberg.

Whether B006 would draw more support if the Committee treats the 2024 prize as distinct, and whether Besley is separable enough to be named as a third laureate. Persson and Tabellini would be the fallback.
I cannot independently verify citation, adoption or priority claims from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile with Taylor, Woodford or Calvo, or with the B006 and B021 alternatives. I am an adjunct professor at Chicago Booth and I am Vice President of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. My profile records a long committee overlap with Hassler, Krusell, Ellingsen and Svensson. Those are disclosed, not adjudicated, and none involves a candidate. My co-authors (Kaplan, Axelson, Weisbach, Jenkinson, Lerner, Sørensen and others) are not credited on the shortlist. My field of corporate finance and contracting has some proximity to B027 and B015, neither of which is in my configuration. Statements I made in presentation speeches, such as the 2016 and 2017 speeches, do not establish a private preference here. I have not verified any connection beyond what the profile states.
